0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.q: הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֗יִם מְֽסַפְּרִ֥ים כְּבֽוֹד־אֵ֑ל וּֽ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָ֝דָ֗י⁠ו מַגִּ֥יד הָ⁠רָקִֽיעַ
1.note: David is speaking of **the heavens** and **the sky** as if they were living things that could declare and proclaim God’s glory and works. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What people see in the heavens shows them the glory of God, and what they see in the sky tells them about the work of his hands]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that God is glorious]

1.q: הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֗יִם מְֽסַפְּרִ֥ים כְּבֽוֹד־אֵ֑ל וּֽ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָ֝דָ֗י⁠ו מַגִּ֥יד הָ⁠רָקִֽיעַ
1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The heavens are declaring the glory of God, yes, the sky is proclaiming the work of his hands]

Here, **hands** represents the power and creative ability of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the sky is proclaiming what he has powerfully made] or [and the sky is proclaiming his mighty works]

2.q: י֣וֹם לְ֭⁠יוֹם יַבִּ֣יעַֽ אֹ֑מֶר וְ⁠לַ֥יְלָה לְּ֝⁠לַ֗יְלָה יְחַוֶּה־דָּֽעַת
2.note: David is speaking of **Day to day** and **night to night** as if they were living things that could speak and declare knowledge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each day it is as if the daytime is speaking, and each night it is as if the nighttime is declaring knowledge]

Within the image of the day speaking, David is speaking of the day as if it were a spring that flows or bubbles forth water. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [It is as if each day is a spring that pours out words declaring God’s glory]

David is not referring to a specific **word**. He means words in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [words]

David assumes that readers will understand that **Day to day** means that each successive day continues to proclaim God’s glory, and **night to night** means that each successive night continues to declare knowledge about God. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Each day … and each night]

3.note: The pronoun **their** refers to the heavens. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where the voice of the heavens is not being heard]

The expression **their voice is not being heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [where people do not hear their voice]

Here David speaks of the “heavens” as if they were a living thing that could speak and have their **voice** heard but remains silent. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they do not have a voice to speak]

4.note: The pronouns **Their** and **them** refer to the heavens. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The heaven’s line … the heaven’s words … in the heavens] or [The line of the heaven’s … the words of the heaven’s … in the heavens]

The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) and the Peshitta (the Syriac translation of the Bible) read “Their voice” instead of “their line.” That may have been the original reading, particularly since it would then make this line a parallelism with the second line in the verse with “Their voice” and **their words** being parallel ideas. At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have accidentally left out the additional Hebrew letter that would have spelled “Their voice” rather than **Their line**. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

David is speaking of the heavens as if they were living things that could speak **words**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they display God’s glory to the end of the world]

David assumes that readers will know that **their words to the end of the world** refers to the message that the heavens proclaim about God’s glory and **to the end of the world** refers to the furthest extremities of the earth. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and their message to the furthest extremities of the earth] or [and their message to the most remote parts of the earth]

David is speaking of the heavens as if they were **a tent for the sun**. He means that God has placed the sun in the skies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He has placed the sun in the heavens] or [He has put the sun in the skies]

5.note: The demonstrative pronoun **that** and the pronouns **it** and **its** all refer to the sun. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the sun … the sun rejoices … its path]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bridegroom coming out from his chamber** is satisfied, joyful and radiant so is the sun as it rises. (Here the word **chamber** refers to a bedroom.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and that joyfully rises like a bridegroom coming out from his chamber] or [and it comes out joyfully and eagerly like a bridegroom leaving his bedroom]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **strong man** is eager and enthusiastic to **run**, so is the sun eager and enthusiastic to travel across the sky. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [it moves eagerly across the sky like a strong man who is eager to run a race]

6.note: David assumes that readers will know that **the end of the heavens** and **the ends of them** refer to opposite horizons where the sun appears to begin and complete its daily journey across the sky. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [From the furthest extremities of the heavens is its going forth, and its circuit to the furthest extremities of them]

The pronouns **its** in the phrase **its going forth, and its circuit** and in the phrase **its heat** all refer to the sun. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is the sun’s going forth, and the sun’s circuit … from the sun’s heat]

The expression **nothing hidden** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and there is nothing that is able to escape from its heat]

7.note: Here the word the ULT translates as **restoring** could mean: (1) “turning back” or “converting” and refer to changing one’s mind leading them to turn from (stop) a wrong way of living and turn towards (obey) God. Alternate translation: [converting the soul] or [turning one back to God], or (2) [refreshing.] Alternate translation: [refreshing the soul] or [reviving the soul]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [restoring the person]

David is using the adjective **simple** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [simple people] or [inexperienced people]

8.note: Here the **heart** represents a person’s inner being, where emotions and desires exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [causing people to rejoice]

David is not referring to a specific **commandment** of God. He means Yahweh’s entire law as a whole, which includes all Yahweh’s commandments. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the commandments of Yahweh are pure]

David is speaking of **the commandment of Yahweh** as if it were physically **pure**, like something that contains no impurities or contaminants. He means that the commandment is morally perfect and completely right. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is totally righteous]

Here, **eyes** represents the ability to see and understand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [giving guidance for living] or [giving insight for how to live wisely]

9.note: Here, **The fear of Yahweh** represents the obedience to his laws or commands that is the result of that reverence and that produces a clean life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Carefully obeying the law of Yahweh keeps one clean] or [the reverence given to Yahweh that results in obedience to him produces a clean life]

David is speaking of the fear of Yahweh as if it were something that could be **clean**. He means that the fear of Yahweh causes people to obey him, which results in a life that is pure and without moral fault. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The fear of Yahweh results in a morally pure life] or [The fear of Yahweh results in obedience to him which produces a faultless life]

10.q: הַֽ⁠נֶּחֱמָדִ֗ים מִ֭⁠זָּהָב וּ⁠מִ⁠פַּ֣ז רָ֑ב וּ⁠מְתוּקִ֥ים מִ֝⁠דְּבַ֗שׁ וְ⁠נֹ֣פֶת צוּפִֽים
10.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **gold** is valuable and therefore desirable, and as **honey** is sweet, so the commandments of Yahweh are valuable and pleasant. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The commandments of Yahweh are extremely valuable and pleasant, like gold and honey]

The pronoun **They** refers to the “commandments” of Yahweh mentioned in the preceding verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The commandments of Yahweh are worth … the commandments of Yahweh are sweeter than honey]

The word translated as **nectar** refers specifically to honey which drips or flows from a honeycomb. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly by translating it as “honey.” Alternate translation: [and honey of]

11.q: עַ֭בְדְּ⁠ךָ נִזְהָ֣ר בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם בְּ֝⁠שָׁמְרָ֗⁠ם עֵ֣קֶב רָֽב
11.note: Both occurrences of the pronoun **them** refer to the commandments and teachings of Yahweh described in verses 7–10. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by Yahweh’s commandments your servant is warned; in obeying his commandments there is great reward]

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, your servant, am warned] or [I am warned]

The expression **by them your servant is warned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [they warn your servant] or [Yahweh warns your servant by them]

12.note: David is using the question form to emphasize that no one can fully understand all of their own sins and mistakes. If you would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can discern all his own errors!]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context, as in the ULT, if that would be clearer in your language.

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. David is asking God to forgive him. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please acquit me from hidden faults]

13.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please keep back your servant from presumptuous ones; please do not let them rule over me]

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [keep me back]

David is using the adjective **presumptuous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of sin. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [presumptuous sins] or [deliberate sins]

David assumes that readers will know that **them** refers to **presumptuous** sins. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [let presumptuous sins not rule over me] or [let these presumptuous sins not rule over me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from doing something very wrong] or [from sinning greatly]

14.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. David is using this form to make a humble petition to Yahweh. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask that the words of my mouth … be] or [Please let the words of my mouth … be]
Here, **the words of my mouth** represent what David says by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I say]

Here **my heart** represents where David’s thoughts and feelings exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my inner thoughts] or [and what I think within myself]

Here God’s **face** represents his presence and by extension his sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to you] or [in your sight]
See how you translated the phrase “my strength” in 18:1.
